title: When THE POPULIST meets THE HEGEMON:
subtitle: The Dialectic of the Streets

script.text: In a crowded marketplace where history is sold by the pound, two figures struggle over a megaphone. One is THE POPULIST (representing the "Descriptive" view of Culture). He wears a cap and holds a vast inventory list. He believes that popular culture is simply whatever the people do—pigeon-fancying, stamp-collecting, reading the Daily Mirror.

script.speaker: THE Populist
script.text: This is the culture of the people. It is authentic. It is theirs. We must celebrate it. If the people buy it, it is popular. If they enjoy it, it is good

The other figure is THE HEGEMON (representing Dominant Ideology/Cultural Imperialism). He wears a suit and holds a red pen. He believes that popular culture is a mechanism of control, a way to educate and reform the masses into obedience.

script.speaker: THE Hegemon
script.text: The people do not create this culture; they consume it. I reconstructed their press in the 19th century. I gave them the Daily Mirror. I taught them to be "patriotic." Their culture is not an enclave; it is a battlefield I have already won. They are cultural dopes, doped on the opium of the media
A third figure steps out from the shadows. It is THE THEORIST (representing Stuart Hall/Cultural Studies). He wears no costume, but carries a history book covering the years 1880-1920.

script.speaker: THE Theorist
script.text: You, Populist, ignore power. You think culture is a self-contained world. But there is no "authentic" popular culture outside the field of force. And you, Hegemon, underestimate resistance. The people are not screens; they are active. They do not just absorb; they negotiate
The Theorist points to a swastika dangling from a punk rocker's neck.

script.speaker: THE Theorist
script.text: Is he a fascist? Or is he mocking you? The sign is not fixed. It is a site of struggle. Meaning is not inscribed in the object; it is won or lost in the conflict

script.speaker: THE CROWD
script.text: Popular culture is neither pure resistance nor pure domination

script.speaker: THE Theorist
script.text: It is the ground on which the transformations are worked. It is the "Double Movement" of containment and resistance. The magistrate and the police are part of the history of popular culture. Reform is as important as riot

script.speaker: THE POPULIST
script.text: The people are not a fixed subject

script.speaker: THE HEGEMON
script.text: They are a prize to be won. Mrs. Thatcher says, "This is what the people want." She is constructing "The People" as a political force. We must do the same. Popular culture matters not because it is intrinsically good, but because it is one of the places where socialism might be constituted. It is the stake in the game
